draft.title: Hindu sexual ethics
card: Many Hindu texts place sexuality within marriage (vivaha), which is seen as a sacred duty and a stage of life. Sexual relations are linked to dharma, the duty and right conduct a person owes at their stage of life.

In the four stages of life (ashramas), the householder stage (grihastha) is where marriage, family and children have a central place. The student stage (brahmacharya) is linked with self-control and study.
Hindu teachings often count kama, or pleasure and desire, as a legitimate aim of life (purusharthas), when it is pursued in line with dharma. It is not treated as wrong in itself.
Hindus do not all hold the same view. Attitudes to topics such as dating, contraception and same-sex relationships differ across communities, traditions and between traditional and modern outlooks.
draft.remember: Many Hindus see sexuality as belonging within marriage and dharma, but views vary across communities.

a.q: Which statement best describes how many Hindu teachings treat kama, or desire, in relation to sexuality?
opts: A legitimate aim of life when pursued in line with dharma
A wrong that a person must remove at every stage of life
An aim that matters more than dharma during married life
A private matter that has no link to duty or right conduct
a.why: Kama is one of the purusharthas, so desire is treated as a proper aim when it fits dharma. It is not treated as wrong in itself, and it is not placed outside duty or above it.
a.clue: Think of kama as one aim of life that dharma guides.

b.q: Two Hindu families in Sydney, from different communities, hold different views on dating and contraception. What does this best show about Hindu sexual ethics?
opts: Views differ across communities, even with shared themes
One family must be wrong, as the texts give one rule
Hindu teaching has no link between sexuality and dharma
Only the family with the older traditions is truly Hindu
b.why: Hindu teaching shares themes such as marriage and dharma, but communities and traditions apply them in different ways. The idea of one fixed rule is tempting, but Hinduism has no single authority that sets one view for all Hindus.
b.clue: Shared themes can still be applied in different ways.

a.best: A legitimate aim of life when pursued in line with dharma

b.best: Views differ across communities, even with shared themes

problems.detail: All three wrong options are extreme or absolute ('must be wrong', 'Only the family...', 'no link'). The right option is the only measured one and echoes the card's 'views vary across communities', so a Year 12 student could pick it without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The facts on vivaha, the ashramas, kama as a purushartha and the diversity of views are accurate, and both intended answers are correct. Question b is too easy to guess because its wrong options are all extreme absolutes, which makes the right answer stand out.

b.q: Two Hindu families in Sydney, both in the householder stage, come from different communities. Both see marriage as the place for sexuality, but they differ on dating and contraception. What does this best show?
opts: Shared ideals of marriage and dharma are applied differently
One family has set aside dharma in favour of modern values
Dating and contraception sit outside Hindu ideas of dharma
The families are in different stages of life, or ashramas
b.why: Both families keep the shared ideal of sexuality within marriage, yet their communities apply it differently to dating and contraception. It is tempting to think one family has dropped dharma, but both still hold the ideal linked to it, and both are in the same stage of life.
b.clue: Look at what the families agree on before what they differ on.
